items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Stock Market Trend Prediction and Risk Assessment: A Review
items.abstract: Machine learning models are now widely used to forecast stock price movements and to measure financial risk, yet most cannot explain their own outputs. In finance that is a serious weakness, because forecasts influence real investment decisions and regulators expect firms to justify the models they use. This review asks how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been applied to stock trend prediction and risk as-sessment, and how far the resulting explanations can be trusted. We first outline the economic theory of predictability and the standard risk measures, then set out the mathematics of the main explanation methods: Shapley-value attribution, LIME, gradient-based attribution, attention, and counterfactuals. We then compare representative studies, summarise regulatory expectations, and propose a five-layer framework for explainable forecasting. Across the literature we find that explanations are most useful as a validation tool, and that they become un-reliable when features are correlated, when markets change regime, or when a model is overfitted. Evidence that expla-nations improve decisions remains thin. We close with open problems, including causal explanation, shared benchmarks, and monitoring of explanations in production.

items.title: Explainable deep learning for stroke lesion analysis: CNN, transformer, hybrid models, and future directions: a systematic review
items.abstract: Abstract Background Stroke is the second leading cause of death and the third leading cause of disability worldwide, affecting approximately 15 million people annually and imposing an economic burden exceeding US$890 billion. Interpretation of brain CT and MRI images is time-consuming, subject to inter-observer variability, and limited by a shortage of neuroradiology experts, particularly in low-resource settings. Deep learning methods have shown strong potential for automated stroke lesion analysis; however, the rapid emergence of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), transformers, and hybrid architectures requires systematic evaluation. Objectives This systematic review summarizes recent advances in CNN-based, transformer-based, and hybrid CNN–transformer models for stroke lesion segmentation and classification using CT and MRI. It also evaluates diagnostic performance, examines explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, identifies barriers to clinical translation, and outlines future research directions. Methods Studies published between 1 January 2015 and 15 January 2026 were identified through searches of IEEE Xplore, PubMed, Scopus, and SpringerLink. Study quality was assessed using the Stroke AI Quality Assessment (SAI-QA) tool, with 48 studies (64.0%) rated as high quality (Cohen’s κ = 0.80). Due to heterogeneity in datasets, methods, and evaluation metrics, meta-analysis was not performed. Results CNN-based models were most commonly used (56%), with U-Net variants achieving Dice scores of 0.59–0.94 for segmentation. Transformer-based models (24%) achieved classification accuracies up to 99.6% and Dice scores above 0.90 by capturing long-range dependencies. Hybrid CNN–transformer models (16%) generally outperformed individual architectures by combining local and global feature learning. Explainable AI methods such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME were reported in only 11% of studies, and there was no standardized evaluation framework. Key challenges included class imbalance (24%), limited annotated data (20%), poor generalization across institutions (16%), and computational complexity (11%). Emerging approaches such as federated learning (4%), self-supervised learning (5%), and few-shot learning (3%) showed promise for addressing data limitations and privacy concerns. Clinical implications Hybrid CNN–Transformer models show strong potential for clinical stroke diagnosis by combining local feature extraction with global context understanding. However, limited external validation, poor Explainability, and high computational cost remain key barriers to real-world clinical use. Conclusion Hybrid CNN–transformer architectures currently provide the best balance between accuracy and robustness for stroke lesion analysis. However, Explainability remains underdeveloped, and standardized evaluation frameworks are lacking. Future research should focus on multi-center validation, standardized benchmarking, uncertainty-aware XAI, federated learning, and equitable deployment in low-resource settings. This review guides advancing clinically translatable AI systems in stroke imaging.

items.abstract: Modern law enforcement agencies face the dual challenge of managing complex public safety threats while maintaining strict institutional accountability. This paper explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and advanced digital tools within modern policing frameworks. By analyzing current implementations—including predictive policing algorithms, automated facial recognition, automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and AI-driven evidence management systems—this study assesses how these technologies enhance operational efficiency, accelerate response times, and optimize resource allocation. Furthermore, the paper addresses critical systemic challenges, specifically targeting algorithmic bias, citizen privacy concerns, data security vulnerabilities, and the regulatory frameworks required to govern automated decision-making. Ultimately, this research provides a balanced framework for law enforcement executives and policymakers, demonstrating how agencies can leverage cutting-edge technical innovation while upholding the core principles of ethical, transparent, and community-oriented justice

items.title: Face Mood Detection Using Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Face Mood Detection Using Artificial Intelligence is a web-based application developed to recognize human emotions from facial expressions using Artificial Intelligence (AI), Deep Learning and Computer Vision techniques. The application provides a secure user authentication system using Firebase Authentication, allowing users to register, log in and create a personal profile, which is stored in the Firebase Realtime Database. After successful login, users can detect their emotions using three input methods: Browser Camera, Local Webcam or Image Upload. The system uses OpenCV for face detection and a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model developed with TensorFlow/Keras to classify facial expressions into six emotions: Happy, Sad, Angry, Fear, Neutral and Disgust. The application is built with Streamlit, providing an interactive interface for emotion detection. Along with the detected emotion, the system displays the prediction confidence score and personalized AI-generated emotional insights. As an additional feature, it provides music and movie suggestions based on the detected mood, enhancing user interaction with suitable entertainment recommendations. By integrating AI, image processing, cloud-based services and recommendation features, the project demonstrates a practical and user-friendly approach to facial emotion recognition, with potential applications in emotional well-being awareness, education, healthcare, human-computer interaction and smart assistance systems. Keywords: Facial Emotion Recognition, Artificial Intelligence, Deep Learning, Convolutional Neural Network, OpenCV, Computer Vision, Streamlit, Firebase, Mood-Based Recommendation.

items.title: Factorial Structure and Measurement Invariance of the Sport Satisfaction Instrument Adapted to Physical Education in Mexican Adolescents
items.abstract: Instructional activities that satisfy basic psychological needs can promote enjoyment and intrinsic motivation in learning. This instrumental study assessed the psychometric properties of the Spanish-adapted Sport Satisfaction Instrument (SSI-PE) within the context of physical education and examined its measurement invariance across sex among Mexican students. Participants included a total of 515 secondary school students from the cities of Chihuahua, Aldama, and Cuauhtémoc in the State of Chihuahua, Mexico; of these, 259 (50.3%) were males and 256 (49.7%) were females, and their ages ranged between 12 and 15 years (M = 13.15, SD = 0.86). Confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance by sex, and calculation of Pearson’s correlation coefficients were conducted to assess convergent validity. The seven-item model, the SSI-PE7, demonstrated more robust fit indices (GFI = 0.985, RMSEA = 0.047, and CFI = 0.990) and acceptable reliability (α = 0.84 for the satisfaction/fun factor and α = 0.74 for boredom). Measurement invariance analysis evidenced its applicability regardless of sex. Convergent validity showed that satisfaction/fun had a positive correlation with task orientation and ego, while the boredom factor had a negative correlation with the other scales. The findings suggest that the SSI-PE7 is a promising and reliable provisional instrument to assess students’ level of satisfaction with physical education classes.

items.title: Federated, Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Heart Disease Prediction: A Literature Synthesis and a Proposed SHAP-Based Framework
items.abstract: Heart disease is still the world's biggest killer, responsible for an estimated 19.8 million deaths in 2022 up from the 17.9 million figures for 2019 that gets cited so often in older papers.Machine learning models have gotten quite good at predicting cardiovascular risk, but two problems keep them out of the clinic: nobody can easily explain why a model flagged a given patient, and hospitals cannot legally pool their data to train better models in the first place.This paper looks at how federated learning (FL) and explainable AI (XAI) are being combined to deal with both problems at once, drawing on a review of twenty-eight peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2026 that apply FL, ensemble learning, or XAI methods such as SHAP and LIME to cardiovascular data.Building on the gaps that review turns up, we propose FedX-Heart, a framework pairing a federated ensemble of Random Forest, XGBoost, and LSTM models with layered privacy protection (differential privacy, secure aggregation, k-anonymity) and dual SHAP/LIME explanations.The studies reviewed here report that federated training can match centralized accuracy (92.3% versus 90.1%), that stacking ensembles beat individual base learners (91-98% accuracy), that a transfer-learning ensemble reaches 98.2% accuracy with SHAP interpretability built in, and that adding k-anonymity costs only a few points of accuracy (83.21%).A synthesis of feature-importance findings across six SHAP-based studies turns up solid agreement on some predictors and real disagreement on others, and lining FedX-Heart up against its three closest predecessors shows that none of them covers federation, accuracy, privacy, and generalizability all at once.Taken together, it shows that relationship mastery and explanatory AI can blend out and deliver a lot of accuracy, though open questions remain around how privacy noise affects causes, how badly non-IID medical laboratory data hurts things in practice, and whether those protections penalize small patient subgroups.Even the FedX-Heart is a proposed design and not something we have tried, yet all need empirical validation before it should be clinically agreed upon.

items.title: Fifty. Serie Cuentos de Papel Capítulo I
items.abstract: Fifty es un cuento breve de ficción sobre un glosario de 1512, vanidoso y clasista, que vive en el sótano de una biblioteca de Alabama convencido de que los dioses vendrán a buscarlo. Cuando lo sacan de la sala, el libro cree que ha llegado su apoteosis. Lo que llega es un escáner, una guillotina y un informe. A través de la voz de un objeto que se siente elegido, el relato explora cómo los sistemas de inteligencia artificial se alimentan de la memoria escrita de la humanidad, y qué ocurre con el soporte, la historia y las huellas humanas una vez que el contenido ha sido digitalizado y se considera redundante. El texto dialoga con "La noche boca arriba", de Julio Cortázar, e incorpora un informe técnico final que contrasta con el tono fabulesco del resto. Es el primer capítulo de la serie "Cuentos de papel". Fifty is a short work of fiction about a vain, class-conscious 1512 glossary, kept in the basement of an Alabama library and convinced that the gods will come for him. When he is finally taken from the room, he believes it is his apotheosis. What awaits him is a scanner, a guillotine and a report. Told through an object that thinks itself chosen, the story examines how artificial intelligence systems are fed on humanity's written memory, and what becomes of the physical book, its history and its human traces once its content has been digitized and deemed redundant. The text engages with Julio Cortázar's "La noche boca arriba" and closes with a cold technical report that contrasts with its fable-like tone. It is the first installment of the series "Cuentos de papel".

items.abstract: Let’s be honest: being a college student usually means dealing with some pretty messy money situations. We’re all trying to watch our spending and stick to a budget, but those last-minute splurges always seem to find us. This paper dives into those everyday struggles and suggests FinAI as a simple solution. The idea is to use AI and machine learning to automatically log expenses and give us financial tips that actually make sense for our lives. Basically, if we pair basic money smarts with this kind of tech, we can stop stressing about our bank accounts and start making choices that set us up for the future.

items.title: FINANCIAL DATA ANALYTICS: APPLICATIONS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND MACHINE LEARNING
items.abstract: Financial data analytics uses data analysis techniques to understand financial activities, support decisions, identify risks, and detect unusual transactions. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)have expanded its use in fraud detection, stock-market analysis, bankruptcy prediction, portfolio management, and business forecasting. This paper presents a focused survey of three published review studies: a 2022 bibliometric review of AI and ML in finance, a 2024 literature review on machine-learning-based financial fraud detection, and a 2024 review of ML in business and finance. The studies are compared to identify common applications, methods, benefits, limitations, and future research directions. The reviewed literature indicates growing research interest in AI/ML for financial decision support, a strong role for fraud detection, and increasing use of supervised and deep-learning methods. However, practical implementation continues to face challenges involving data quality, imbalanced datasets, explainability, privacy, model drift, and regulatory compliance. Since this paper synthesizes three selected review articles rather than conducting a new systematic search of all available publications, itsfindings should be interpreted as a focused overview. The paper concludes that responsible, transparent, and regularly monitored AI/ML systems can strengthen financial analytics when combined with human oversight.

items.title: Financial Risk Management in the Digital Era: Cybersecurity, FinTech Innovation, and Banking Sector Resilience
items.abstract: The financial services landscape has witnessed rampant digital change, which has restructured financial risk management and made it a fundamentally new phenomenon. The use of financial technology (FinTech), artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, mobile banking, digital payments systems and data driven financial services brings benefits to financial institutions' operational efficiency and financial inclusion, and boosts their ability to develop and launch financial products. But these factors have also brought additional challenges, among them cyber-attacks, data breaches and digital fraud, reliance on third-party technologies, algorithmic bias, system disruption and vulnerabilities. Therefore, traditional risk management approaches are becoming less effective in tackling the interrelated risks of today's banking environment. Here, we review how cybersecurity, FinTech innovation and banking sector resilience are related in the digital era. The study is based on la COUNT qualitative second data analytical approach with englobing existing literature, regulatory frameworks and principles of institutional risk management. It delves into the evolving characteristics of credit, market, liquidity, operational and systemic risks in a digital world and assesses the significance of cybersecurity governance and regulatory compliance, technological innovation, and organisational resilience. Overall, the analysis suggests that technology-assisted financial transformation can enhance the stability of the financial system with strong governance, the use of effective cyber-risk management measures, responsible innovation and adequate regulatory oversight. The article suggests that integrated risk management frameworks, the monitoring of threats on an ongoing basis, scenario-based stress testing, the use of third-party risk assessment, employee education and cross-border regulatory co-operation should all be introduced. It concludes that this financial inclusion for sustainability in digital finance will need a balance of innovation, security, accountability, and resilience on the side of the financial institutions.

items.title: From Clinical Question to Defensible Inference: A Decision Framework for Integrated Gut Microbiome–Metabolome Studies
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid expansion of microbiome and metabolome technologies has transformed the study of host-microbial interactions, but methodological choices are still often driven by technical availability rather than by the question and intended claim. This review examines how biological compartment, microbiome profiling, metabolomics platform, data-integration strategy and validation determine the strength of inference in integrated gut microbiome–metabolome research. We distinguish descriptive association from functional interpretation, clinical prediction and causal evidence, and identify the analytical safeguards required for credible biomarker development. We then propose a five-stage decision framework that begins with definition of the intended scientific or clinical claim, links that claim to compartment and analytical resolution, selects integration according to purpose, and limits interpretation to the achieved validation level. Building on recent calls for question-driven multi-omics integration, its practical contribution is to connect prospective design choices to the intended claim and make the weakest validated component of the analytical chain — rather than technology choice alone — the explicit ceiling for the permissible claim, illustrated by two worked design examples. This question-driven approach is intended to improve design transparency, reproducibility and the responsible clinical translation of integrated microbiome–metabolome studies.

items.title: From Content Transmission to Epistemic Construction: Redesigning University Education in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence challenges the university model centered on content transmission and subsequent testing. Large language models can retrieve, synthesize, and recombine information within seconds, but rapid access to information does not constitute reliable knowledge. This conceptual article argues that higher education should shift toward epistemic construction: the process of framing problems, integrating information, verifying sources, exposing assumptions, confronting counterarguments, revising provisional judgments, and defending conclusions. Drawing on Socratic inquiry, medieval disputatio, Popperian falsification, reflective learning, critical-thinking research, and scholarship on artificial intelligence in education, the study proposes the AI-Assisted Epistemic Construction Cycle. The framework positions generative AI not primarily as an answer-producing device, but as a scalable digital devil’s advocate that supports structured intellectual dissent. Implications are developed for faculty roles, student agency, assessment, institutional governance, academic integrity, and future research.

items.title: From Critical Thinking Disposition to Learning Engagement: The Roles of Motivation, Academic Buoyancy, and Grit in AI ‐Supported University Learning
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence is changing university students' learning experiences, but how cognitive dispositions translate into sustained engagement in AI‐supported learning remains insufficiently understood. Guided by the Study Demands–Resources Model, this study examines the association between critical thinking disposition and learning engagement, with learning motivation, academic buoyancy, and grit as parallel indirect pathways. Using cross‐sectional data from 729 university students with experience using AI for learning, structural equation modelling tested the direct and indirect relationships among the variables, after which psychological network analysis identified central and bridge nodes within the learning psychological system. Critical thinking disposition was conceptualised as a cognitive personal resource, and learning motivation as a motivational resource. Academic buoyancy captured students' capacity to manage everyday academic setbacks, whereas grit represented perseverance in pursuing long‐term learning goals. The combination of variable‐centred and network‐based analyses provided complementary views of how these resources relate to university students' engagement in AI‐supported learning.

items.title: From Dentists to AI: Oral Health Information-seeking Behavior Among Pregnant Women in the Digital Era—A Cross-sectional Study
items.abstract: Introduction Pregnancy is a critical period during which optimal oral health is essential for maternal and fetal well-being. With increasing use of digital technologies, pregnant women obtain oral health information from various sources, including healthcare professionals, social media, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based platforms. This study assessed oral health information-seeking behavior among pregnant women and its association with oral health knowledge. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 150 pregnant women attending antenatal clinics in Vijayawada. Data were collected using a structured self-administered questionnaire. Descriptive statistics and Chi-square tests were used for analysis, with statistical significance set at p < .05. Results The mean age of participants was 28.42 ± 5.07 years. Although 96.7% had internet access, only 34.0% sought oral health information during pregnancy. Dentists were the most commonly used and trusted source (45.0%), followed by obstetricians (23.5%), while social media and AI chatbots were each used by 11.7%. Preferred information source was significantly associated with knowledge of gum disease ( p < .001), the safety of dental treatment ( p = .018), and the impact of maternal oral health on the baby’s health ( p = .040). Information-seeking behavior was also associated with better knowledge of gum disease ( p < .001) and the importance of regular dental check-ups during pregnancy ( p < .001). Conclusion Despite widespread internet access, oral health information-seeking during pregnancy was limited. Professional guidance, particularly from dentists, was associated with better oral health knowledge, emphasizing the need to strengthen evidence-based oral health education within antenatal care.

items.title: From Foundation to Frontier: Re-Examining Bloom’s Taxonomy Across the Four Levels of Education in ICT and Generative AI Era
items.abstract: Bloom’s Taxonomy remains one of the most enduring pedagogical frameworks in global education, offering a structured hierarchy of cognitive processes from Remembering to Creating. In the age of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and generative artificial intelligence (AI), its relevance has been both reinforced and problematised. This article argues that the effectiveness of Bloom’s Taxonomy is not uniform across the four levels of education—Primary, Secondary, Higher Secondary, and Tertiary—but rather varies in emphasis and application according to students’ cognitive development, curricular demands, and the affordances of digital tools. Drawing on contemporary scholarship and the Bangladeshi educational context, the article proposes a differentiated model of Bloom’s application, where lower-order cognitive skills (LOCS) dominate early schooling while higher-order cognitive skills (HOCS) become progressively central. It further contends that Bloom’s Taxonomy, while necessary, is insufficient in the AI era unless complemented by digital literacy, AI literacy, ethical reasoning, and process-oriented assessment. The article concludes with implications for curriculum design, teacher development, and assessment reform.

items.title: From Molecules to Medicines
items.abstract: Drug discovery takes a long time, usually 10 to 15 years. It also costs more than USD 2 billion for each approved drug, with clinical failure rates close to 90%. Traditional linear processes find it hard to tackle complicated issues like chronic diseases, antimicrobial resistance, and new health threats. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are goal-directed structures that combine large language models, reinforcement learning, and multi-agent setups. They allow for fully automated, closed-loop drug discovery. These AI systems can identify targets, create and improve molecules, design and run experiments in robotic labs, and continuously change strategies based on real-time feedback. Even with their ability to cut down on time, costs, and failure rates, challenges still exist related to understanding, data bias, ethics, and regulatory oversight.

items.title: From Search to Co-Planning: How Vietnamese Independent Travelers Use, Verify, And Act on Generative Ai Recommendations
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how travelers search for information and plan trips, yet much of the existing research still focuses on technology adoption, trust, or continuance intentions rather than on the process through which an AI recommendation is checked and translated into an actual decision. This study explores how Vietnamese independent travelers use GenAI in trip planning, how they evaluate and verify AI outputs, and how they decide whether to accept, modify, or reject those recommendations. An exploratory qualitative design was employed, involving 28 participants who had used GenAI to plan a specific independent trip. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews and analyzed using the Gioia methodology. The findings suggest that GenAI is shifting from a search tool toward a co-planning partner; however, its outputs are rarely received entirely passively. Travelers engage in selective verification depending on perceived risk, information volatility, and decision reversibility, while calibrating their trust according to the task and prior experience. Four ways of integrating AI recommendations into travel decisions were identified: direct acceptance, acceptance after verification, modified acceptance, and rejection. The study therefore proposes the concept of “verified co-planning” and develops a process model in which verification and trust calibration connect AI recommendations with action. These findings extend process-based understanding of GenAI in tourism and clarify how travelers preserve agency as AI becomes more deeply embedded in travel planning.

items.title: From Thought to Thwaction: Where Thoughts Come From, How They Become Action, and What They Are Worth
items.abstract: Research on human thinking explains how thoughts arise and how decisions are made, but rarely asks how a thought becomes an action, how the way thinking begins can be trained, and what a thought is worth. This conceptual paper answers these questions from Kirdomicism, an action-centric philosophy. It introduces the thwaction, a thorough thought carried by will into effective action, with accountability for its result, summarised in the conceptual equation Thinking × Action = Avalrem, where Avalrem is the unit of action value. The paper argues that a decision is not the end of thinking but the middle of an action; that self-force, willpower developed into habit, carries thought into action; that thoughts arise from a life setting described by the Buddhist Five Aggregates, with each first thought unpredictable but the mind’s tendencies trainable through a tool-free daily thwaction cycle; and that a thought has no value until it becomes action. The paper engages research on the intention–behaviour gap, implementation intentions, habit, spontaneous thought, prospection, cognitive offloading to artificial intelligence and the economics of ideas, including proposals to pay people for their data. It offers 23 propositions classified as definitional, explanatory or normative, two new measures (the thwaction count and the thwaction rate), and a research agenda of five studies.

items.title: From Waste to Wealth: Integrating Biological Systems and Molecular Intelligence for Lignin Valorization
items.abstract: Lignin is an abundant and renewable aromatic polymer, but its structural heterogeneity hinders its efficient bioconversion. Unlike previous reviews that focused on isolated topics such as single enzymes, pathway engineering, or specific bioproducts, this paper comprehensively reviews the latest advances in the structural characteristics, microbial degradation mechanisms, and bioconversion of lignin. Particular emphasis is placed on the catalytic mechanisms of key lignin-degrading enzymes, including laccase, lignin peroxidase (LiP), and manganese peroxidase (MnP), as well as the applications of fungi, bacteria, and synthetic microbial consortia in lignin bioconversion. Metabolic pathways that channel heterogeneous lignin-derived aromatics into central carbon metabolism through sequential catalytic reactions are also covered. Furthermore, we evaluate the emerging applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning in enzyme design and bioprocess control. Finally, techno-economic and life-cycle considerations are integrated to guide large-scale deployment. This review provides in-depth insights into the cross-scale translation from laboratory biocatalysis to industrial biorefineries.

items.title: From Weakly Supervised Segmentation to Diagnostic Decisions: An Annotation-Economics Review for Medical Imaging
items.abstract: Accurate medical image segmentation and the diagnostic decisions it supports are increasingly constrained by the cost of supervision: dense voxel-level annotation by expert clinicians remains slow, expensive, and difficult to scale, leaving many anatomies, pathologies, and modalities sparsely labeled. A large literature therefore relaxes the demand for full masks, yet existing surveys often catalog broad forms of limited supervision without directly comparing the practical trade-off between label granularity, annotation burden, and segmentation quality. This review focuses on weakly and coarsely labeled settings (image-level tags, points/clicks, bounding boxes, scribbles, and coarse masks, together with gaze or partial annotations as separate, protocol-dependent forms of supervision) and organizes them through an annotation-economics perspective that considers per-case annotation cost, required expertise, scalability, and the reported performance gap relative to full supervision. The evidence suggests that box and scribble supervision can provide favorable cost–performance trade-offs in several medical segmentation studies, although the reported metrics and datasets are heterogeneous and should not be interpreted as a unified quantitative frontier. We next examine the foundation-model turn, namely the Segment Anything Model and its medical derivatives, and argue that promptable models re-encode rather than eliminate human supervision, moving part of the effort from offline labeling to inference-time interaction. Finally, we extend the analysis beyond Dice to ask whether weakly produced masks support downstream clinical tasks: aggregate measurements may be relatively tolerant of moderate boundary error, whereas texture and high-order radiomic features can be substantially more sensitive. We close by identifying benchmark fragmentation, annotation variability, and the still-limited evidence connecting weak segmentation to clinical outcomes as open problems and propose a unified “weak label → task” benchmark for future evaluation.

items.title: Future Trends in Advanced Building Services: Artificial Intelligence and Smart Technologies Transforming Intelligent Interior Environments
items.abstract: The evolution of advanced building services has significantly transformed contemporary interior environments from passive spatial configurations into intelligent, adaptive, and data-driven ecosystems. Increasing demands for energy efficiency, occupant well-being, sustainability, and operational optimisation have accelerated the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), smart sensors, digital twins, and automated building management systems within architectural and interior design practices. This conceptual review investigates the emerging role of AI and smart technologies in redefining advanced building services and their influence on future interior environments. The study aims to examine the integration of artificial intelligence-based approaches in building performance analysis, environmental control, spatial planning, and occupant-centred design. A qualitative literature review methodology was adopted by analysing recent peer-reviewed studies related to AI-driven building systems, smart building technologies, intelligent environmental controls, and human-centred interior design strategies. The review identifies that AI-enabled systems are increasingly capable of predicting energy demand, analysing occupant behaviour, optimising indoor environmental quality, and supporting adaptive design decisions. The findings indicate that future interior environments will shift from static spaces towards responsive ecosystems capable of learning, predicting, and adapting according to user requirements and environmental conditions. Technologies such as generative AI, digital twins, intelligent lighting, adaptive HVAC systems, and robotic automation are expected to play a significant role in developing sustainable and personalised interiors. However, challenges related to cybersecurity, data privacy, technological dependency, interoperability, and ethical decision-making remain critical concerns. The study concludes that successful implementation of AI-driven building services requires a balanced integration of technological innovation with human creativity, social requirements, and sustainable design principles.

items.title: Future Trends in AI-Driven Sustainability Education and Research
items.abstract: Sustainability is increasingly recognized as a critical component for ensuring a resilient and prosperous future. Its significance spans environmental preservation, economic stability, social equity, and business innovation. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into sustainability education and research is reshaping the landscape of how environmental, social, and economic challenges are understood and addressed. As global sustainability goals become increasingly important and urgent, AI offers the transformative potential to enhance educational practices and research. Several emerging trends are poised to shape the future of AI in sustainability education and research. Firstly, Future trends indicate a shift toward AI-powered personalised learning experiences, where adaptive platforms can tailor content to individual learners’ needs, thereby improving engagement and comprehension. Secondly, the fusion of AI with augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies promises to create immersive learning experiences. These tools can simulate complex environmental scenarios, providing students with interactive platforms to explore sustainability challenges firsthand. Thirdly, AI is increasingly being leveraged to tackle humanitarian and environmental challenges such as the use of Google’s Flood Hub, which forecasts floods in 80 countries, exemplify AI’s potential in enhancing disaster preparedness and response. Fourthly, the interaction of blockchain in AI can enhance data security and transparency in research. This integration ensures the integrity of academic records and facilitates trustworthy collaborations across institutions. Fifthly, AI-driven predictive models can anticipate environmental trends and inform proactive strategies. In education, such analytics can identify at-risk students and tailor interventions to improve retention and success rates. Despite the many potential trends in AI-Driven Sustainability Education and Research , it is important to address ethical concerns such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the potential misuse of technology. Developing responsible future Trends In AI-Driven Sustainability Education and Research requires that technological advancements benefit all stakeholders without causing harm. Institutions must implement frameworks that promote transparency, accountability, and fairness in AI applications, fostering trust and social acceptance. Therefore, incorporating sustainability into AI-driven education equips students with the knowledge and skills necessary to address future environmental challenges.

items.title: Future urgency: who brings politics to the practice of technology? Difficult realities emerging in the AI and technology space
items.abstract: This paper examines who might legitimately bring political considerations into technology development, particularly in contexts where traditional government political actors are absent. Drawing on two generative AI academic-practitioner collaborations in South Africa (a civic participation tool review and a chatbot construction for research content), I draw attention to how digital inequality, funding dynamics, and interpersonal tensions shape knowledge production and decision-making in technology partnerships. The cases demonstrate examples of how technologist knowledge can be undervalued, particularly when it comes to considering the political dimensions of technology deployment. I also consider how poor interpersonal dynamics, which stem from technophobia and discomfort with technical expertise, may have a detrimental impact. These organisational-level challenges have significant implications for emerging AI governance frameworks that rely on collaborative risk assessments and impact evaluations. The paper proposes empathetic collaboration strategies between partners in a technology development process, and strategies that include explicit acknowledgment of inequality in African technology environments, clear communications, skills transfer, and shared normative visions focused on human wellbeing - rather than mere efficiency gains. Such approaches can constitute a resistance to technocapitalist obfuscation and enable more equitable co-creation of responsible AI systems amongst different actors.

items.title: Gender and Academic Level Differences in Artificial Intelligence Usage for Academic Writing in Indonesian Higher Education
items.abstract: The rapid spread of AI chatbots has begun to reshape how university students plan, draft, revise, and evaluate academic writing. Although recent studies have examined students’ perceptions of generative AI in higher education, less is known about how students in regional Indonesian universities understand and use these tools, particularly when viewed across gender, age, and academic level. This study investigated the perceptions and reported use of AI chatbots among 267 students from four universities in East Kalimantan. A mixed-method survey design was used. Quantitative responses were analyzed through descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rho correlation, while open-ended responses were coded to identify the AI tools students reported using for academic writing. The results show that AI use was widespread, with 94.76% of respondents indicating that they had used AI in academic writing. Students generally held positive views of AI chatbots, especially for improving writing effectiveness, language quality, and the revision process. At the same time, their responses revealed continuing ethical and pedagogical uncertainty, particularly around learning, authorship, and the boundary between assistance and cheating. Correlation analysis showed weak relationships between students’ perceptions and gender, age, or semester, suggesting that AI chatbot use was broadly shared across demographic groups. The study offers regional evidence from Indonesian higher education and underscores the need for clearer AI literacy instruction, responsible-use guidelines, and process-based academic writing pedagogy.

items.title: Generating Building Information Models via computer-use agents
items.abstract: Building Information Modeling (BIM) authoring in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector entails navigating complex professional software, demanding significant manual effort and domain expertise. Current automation approaches rely on rigid Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), which detach agents from human-centric visual workflows and limit generalizability across software platforms. This paper presents BIMgent, a multimodal LLM-based agentic framework designed to perform autonomous BIM authoring directly via Graphical User Interface (GUI) interactions. To address high visual noise and long-horizon dependencies, BIMgent incorporates documentation-guided hierarchical planning and dynamic GUI grounding. The framework is evaluated on a benchmark derived from real-world designs of residential buildings. BIMgent achieves a 77.8% end-to-end success rate on long-horizon BIM authoring tasks, significantly outperforming leading generalist computer-use models, including Claude-Sonnet-4.5 (2.2%) and GPT-5.4 (11.1%). By bridging abstract design inputs and concrete modeling actions without API constraints, BIMgent offers a viable path towards autonomous architectural modeling assistants. • A LLM-based multi-agent framework that builds 3D BIM models via GUI, not APIs. • Dynamic GUI grounding, RAG-based planning, and self-reflective execution for GUI-based authoring. • A benchmark of 45 BIM authoring tasks with over 4800 GUI actions. • 77.8% success rate, significantly outperforming leading generalist computer-use models. • A new paradigm for domain-specific LLM agents leveraging human-centric engineering software.

items.title: Generative AI and Copyrightability in the United States: Human Authorship, Creative Control, and AI-Assisted Works
items.abstract: The U.S. Copyright Office has released its report Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability. This paper explores the copyrightability of AI-generated and AI-assisted works in the United States, focusing on that report and on the jurisprudence of human authorship. It examines the constitutional and statutory bases of human authorship, the importance of Burrow-Giles, Feist, Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid and Thaler v. Perlmutter, and how the Copyright Office has dealt with prompting, human-authored inputs, selection, arrangement, modification and the assistive use of AI. The paper shows that the United States has adopted a case-by-case approach: the use of AI as a tool does not defeat protection, but copyright extends only to expression created by a human author and not to material generated by AI itself. Under current technology, prompts alone do not generally provide sufficient control, but human expression that is perceptible in the output, creative selection and arrangement, and meaningful modification can be protected. The paper sets out the strengths and weaknesses of this approach and suggests more explicit registration, evidentiary and guidance practices, while maintaining the human-authorship requirement.

items.title: Generative AI-Based Data Augmentation for Oral Lesion Classification: The PhotoMOCI Dataset and Benchmark
items.abstract: Early detection of oral cancer via photographic imaging presents a promising avenue for large-scale oral cavity screening. However, the development of robust deep learning models is frequently hampered by the scarcity of high-quality, annotated datasets. To address this limitation, a novel and well-curated resource, the Photographic Multi-purpose Oral Cancer Imaging (PhotoMOCI) dataset, is introduced for developing models across multiple diagnostic tasks in oral oncology. Then, a comprehensive benchmark study was conducted to investigate how various data augmentation strategies influence the performance of image classifiers. Our analysis spans different generative AI frameworks, evaluating the efficacy of traditional methods against advanced generative approaches, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Diffusion Models (DMs). Additionally, we propose the Synthetic Image Filter (SIF), a mechanism to select specific samples based on two auxiliary models: Synthetic Proxy Classifier to ensure samples are representative of the target class and Synthetic Image Detector to verify they appear realistic, thereby selecting only the high-utility images that contribute to improving downstream performance. Across the evaluated datasets and classifiers, the best SIF-filtered setup improves accuracy over traditional augmentation in all cases, with gains of +1.73% and +2.35% on PhotoMOCI and +2.38% and +2.08% on KOCD for ResNet50 and ViT, respectively. Our findings reveal that while the direct application of generative data augmentation may yield performance drops, the integration of SIF, considering (i) how synthetic data looks real and (ii) how it reflects the discriminative features of the belonging class, provides a simple yet effective mechanism to filter out synthetic samples that confuse the classifier during training.

items.title: Generative AI-supported problem-based learning for enhancing computational thinking and chemistry achievement in engineering chemistry
items.abstract: The increasing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has created new opportunities to enhance active learning; however, empirical evidence regarding its integration with Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in Engineering Chemistry remains limited, particularly for simultaneously fostering Computational Thinking (CT) and chemistry achievement. This study investigates the effectiveness of integrating GenAI with PBL in an undergraduate Engineering Chemistry course within a Mechanical Engineering Education program. In the intervention, GPT-4 was embedded as an AI learning scaffold that guided students through Socratic questioning, provided formative feedback, and supported problem decomposition and analysis during collaborative PBL activities rather than supplying direct answers. Employing a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design, the study involved 68 undergraduate students (n = 34 experimental; n = 34 control) selected through cluster random sampling. Data were collected using three validated instruments: a Computational Thinking Test (CTT, 30 items, ? = .87), a Chemistry Achievement Test (CAT, 35 items, ? = .84), and a Learning Observation Sheet (LOS, 20 items, ICC = .91). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Levene's homogeneity tests, independent-samples t-tests, ANCOVA, and Cohen's d effect size analysis. The results revealed significant improvements in both CT skills (t(66) = 8.47, p .001) and chemistry achievement (t(66) = 9.12, p .001) in the experimental group compared with the control group. ANCOVA controlling for pretest scores confirmed significant treatment effects for CT (F(1,65) = 127.84, p .001) and chemistry achievement (F(1,65) = 109.07, p .001), with large practical effects (Cohen's d = 2.14 and 2.06, respectively). These findings provide empirical support for integrating AI-supported scaffolding within structured PBL environments to strengthen computational thinking and conceptual understanding in Engineering Chemistry, while extending the pedagogical application of AI-enhanced constructivist learning in engineering education.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Copyright Law in India: Rethinking Authorship, Ownership and Infringement
items.abstract: This paper examines the impact of GenAI technology on India's copyright law, which inherently mandates human authorship. With the help of doctrinal research and surveys among stakeholders, it becomes clear that Indian laws, especially the provision in Section 2(d)(vi) of the Copyright Act, 1957, are insufficient to regulate AI-generated content and data scraping at the stage of training. Important issues in this regard are ownership distribution between creators and end-users of AI and the question whether data scraping for large language models i.e., LLMs is considered a copyright violation or falls under fair use.

items.title: Genomic Foundation Models and De Novo Gene Expression: Transformer DNA Tokenization, Epigenetic Prediction, and Synthetic Sequence Generation
items.abstract: Decoding the regulatory grammar of the human genome and predicting gene expression from primary DNA sequences represent foundational grand challenges in computational biology and synthetic genomics. While traditional bioinformatics pipelines rely on heuristic sequence alignment, position weight matrices (PWMs), and shallow convolutional models, they fail to capture long-range genomic interactions, distal enhancer-promoter looping, and complex epigenetic modifications spanning millions of base pairs. Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs)—large-scale selfsupervised transformer architectures trained on multi-species whole-genome corpora—establish a transformative paradigm shift that treats DNA as a universal biological language. By tokenizing nucleotide sequences into overlapping kmers and training via masked language modeling over ultra-long context windows (up to 1M base pairs), genomic foundation models learn deep representations of splicing sites, transcription factor binding domains, and chromatin accessibility. However, scaling transformer models to whole-genome nucleotide sequences introduces acute mathematical and systems bottlenecks: quadratic self-attention complexity over multi-megabase contexts, high-dimensional embedding collapse across repetitive genomic elements, and poor zero-shot generalization across evolutionary divergences. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of genomic foundation models and de novo gene expression prediction. We formalize nucleotide tokenization and k-mer embedding spaces, derive linear and flash-attention memory bounds for multi-megabase genomic contexts, and model epigenetic chromatin profiling via multi-task transformer heads. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise multi-species benchmark testbed evaluating genomic foundation models (Nucleotide Transformer, Enformer, AlphaGenome) across human gene expression prediction (GTEx v8), pathogenic variant effect scoring (ClinVar), and synthetic promoter generation. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our optimized multi-scale genomic transformer achieves a Pearson correlation of R = 0.892 in predicting cross-tissue gene expression levels from raw DNA sequences alone, while outperforming classical heuristic models by 34.6% in pathogenicity variant effect prediction. Finally, we formulate open challenges in all-genomic generative design, single-cell epigenetic conditioning, and ethical biosecurity screening of synthetic gene constructs.

items.title: GenTile: Closing the Loop Between LLM Reasoning and Physical Telemetry for Autonomous NPU Graph Tuning
items.abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM) hidden widths—such as the 18 944-dimensional intermediate layer of the Qwen family—are often burst-aligned but not tile-compatible with heterogeneous NPU Cube engines, forcing the compiler to emit a small residual kernel that stalls the pipeline for up to 77% of cycles. Manual tuning does not scale across the growing space of model dimensions, sequence lengths, and operator variants. We present GenTile, a dual-role Research–Development (R&D) agent framework that closes the loop between LLM causal reasoning and on-device telemetry: a Research agent diagnoses bottlenecks from structured profiles, a Development agent materializes hardware-legal descriptors from compiler feedback, and iteration traces accumulate into a reusable knowledge base under an air-gap sandbox. On Ascend 910B, an offline hardware-faithful sandbox loop first demonstrates convergence mechanics; on real pretrained weights, the loop then measures the full multi-objective trade-off—latency, energy, memory, AICore efficiency, and approximation error (ε)—across six projection families from two Qwen generations (Qwen3.5-32B and Qwen2.5-7B). From telemetry alone, the agent deploys lossless sibling-projection fusions (QKV, gate–up) consistent with production inference-engine layouts (1.06–1.16× faster, up to 13% lower energy, ε=0, stable across sequence lengths, layer depths, and both models), and rejects every lossy low-rank rewrite—including a 1.39× lm_head speedup whose measured ε=0.89 exceeds any usable accuracy budget—while validating the Eckart–Young cliff prediction (ε → 0.002 at the tail rank) on structural layers. Baselines, ablations, cross-dimension generalization, and a sandbox loop that matches the geometric Oracle within four generations without exhaustive search further support the framework.

items.title: Governance Consequences of Risk-Based AI Regulation: A Comparative Law and Governance Analysis of the EU AI Act and Viet Nam Law
items.abstract: Abstract Risk-based artificial intelligence regulation is usually presented as a settlement between innovation and control. This article instead examines the institutional work that follows when legal systems turn risk into duties, records, review and remedies. It compares Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 with Viet Nam’s Law No. 134/2025/QH15, Decree No. 142/2026/ND-CP, Decision No. 33/2026/QD-TTg on high-risk artificial intelligence (AI) systems and Decree No. 134/2026/ND-CP in the intellectual-property field. The comparison shows that similar risk labels can produce different administrative effects. The EU AI Act is therefore treated not as a model to copy but as a demanding grammar of classification, verification, documentation, supervision, contestation and learning. Viet Nam’s 2026 instruments make the comparison concrete. The article reframes legal borrowing as institutional translation: accountable AI governance depends on procedures through which affected persons can move from harm to forum, evidence and remedy.

items.title: Green AI Strategies for Reducing Energy Consumption and Carbon Emissions in Industrial Systems: Green AI: Industrial Energy and Carbon Reduction
items.abstract: Industrial production depends on electricity, process heat, motors, pumps, compressed-air networks, refrigeration, and production schedules. Artificial Intelligence (AI) can help identify avoidable energy use and support decisions that reduce associated greenhouse-gas emissions. This review examines Green AI strategies for industrial energy and carbon reduction, including energy forecasting, predictive maintenance, process optimisation, intelligent scheduling, digital twins, renewable-energy coordination, and carbon-aware operation. It also considers the environmental cost of AI itself, such as energy used for model training and inference, data storage, networking, and hardware. The reviewed literature indicates that AI-enabled monitoring, prediction, control, scheduling, and parameter optimisation are important application areas. However, reported benefits depend on data quality, system integration, baseline selection, operator acceptance, and verification in real operating conditions. The central research gap is the lack of a consistently applied, independently verifiable framework that measures net energy and carbon benefits across the industrial system while accounting for the AI system’s own footprint and comparing AI with conventional engineering alternatives. This paper organises the gaps, proposes research questions, and presents a practical framework for future work.

items.title: Grounded theory insights into human insider threats: a qualitative study of expert perceptions
items.abstract: Human insider threats continue to increase as digitalization grows, especially with the rise of remote work. Most studies of cybersecurity enhancements focus on technological solutions; however, the costliest cybersecurity events originate from human and insider threat risk factors. This novel, qualitative study identified drivers of human factor insider threats while addressing a need for in-depth, qualitative studies based on expert perceptions. This study conducted semi-structured interviews with 15 cybersecurity experts across government, healthcare, and cybersecurity sectors. A grounded theory methodology strengthened the analysis of codes and themes to generate dominant factors related to drivers and solutions of insider threats that led to developing a Human Insider Threat (HIT) framework. The HIT framework has practical implications for managers to assess insider threat vulnerabilities and for researchers to create scalable instruments to evaluate emerging insider threats. The HIT framework can support organizations in identifying human risk factors, improving security training programs, and aligning technology access controls with employee roles.

items.title: Growing Up Algorithmic
items.abstract: The chapter critically examines how artificial intelligence has transformed children into consumers within the realm of online platforms, toys, and learning systems. It discusses the impact of AI-driven marketing strategies, including recommendation engines and synthetic influencers, on children's preferences and behaviors. The analysis is grounded in theories related to consumer socialization, media psychology, and digital surveillance, exploring how these technologies affect children's cognition, emotional attachments, and decision-making. It highlights concerns over hyper-personalized content, parasocial interactions with AI, and ethical governance regarding data privacy. Additionally, the chapter reviews existing regulatory frameworks, identifies gaps in protecting children, and proposes a holistic approach to understanding the interactions between children and AI. Finally, it advocates for ethical AI design, corporate responsibility, and enhancing AI literacy among parents, contributing to the broader conversation on child rights and digital well-being in an AI-driven era.

items.title: Guidelines for Safe Infusion Practices in Emergency and Acute Care Settings: Society of Acute Care Trauma and Emergency Medicine Delphi Consensus Statement
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Infusion therapy forms an integral part of emergency/acute care medicine, and there continue to be many challenges, such as infusion errors, catheter-related complications, infections, medication errors, and occupational health concerns, in the delivery of safe intravenous therapy. Hence, this Society for Acute Care Trauma and Emergency Medicine guideline sought to provide evidence-based recommendations for safe infusion practices in acute emergency situations. Methodology: A systematic Delphi consensus process was undertaken. The operational definitions for safe infusion practice were defined by the steering committee. Evidence was obtained from searches conducted within PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Database, World Health Organization, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Infusion Nurses Society, Institute for Safe Medication Practices, Joint Commission and other sources. The strength of recommendation was scored using a five-point Likert scale. Results: One hundred and one recommendations were made within 11 categories, which include training and technology, hand hygiene, difficult venous access, peripheral venous catheter insertion and management, infusion processes, infusion technology, prevention of drug administration errors, waste management, training methods and telemedicine/arteficial intelligence. Sixty-three recommendations had reached a high degree of consensus, 24 reached a medium degree of consensus and 14 were considered weak. A total of 55 recommendations reached consensus in the first iteration of the Delphi process, and 46 needed modification/re-evaluation. The scores of agreement were between 72.4% and 97.2%. Conclusions: The recommendations developed by the current study can serve as a systematic and practical approach to ensure infusion safety in the setting of emergency and acute care.

items.title: Holding Kankyo Cafés with the Support and Participation of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The Kankyo (Environment) Café is a dialogue-based forum that fosters mutual understanding and empathy on environmental and social issues through shared learning between researchers and the public. Since 2015, over 200 Cafés have been held in Japan and abroad, including university campuses and public spaces, integrating perspectives from scientific research, the humanities, and daily life. Each Café explores the relationship between nature, society, and human life through themes such as biodiversity, symbiosis, and sustainability, often drawing on literary works like Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring and The Sense of Wonder . During the COVID-19 pandemic, face-to-face meetings transitioned online, expanding accessibility and participation. Since 2022, the National Institute for Environmental Studies (NIES) has hosted regular online Cafés focusing on coexistence with nature, literature, and environmental ethics. In 2024, the Cafés introduced artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, as a participant and co-creator of dialogue content. Monthly online sessions were organized around three main themes: “Considering the Marine Plastics Problem,” “Silent Spring and the Triple Planetary Crisis,” and “Environmental Education.” AI contributed by generating discussion materials and suggesting keywords, while participants reflected on its potential role as an information provider and empathetic interlocutor. Post-session surveys indicated that AI facilitated learning and stimulated awareness of differences in perception, but also highlighted concerns about authenticity and interpretation. The study presents the Café’s philosophy, methods, and outcomes as a model of participatory environmental education that bridges science, ethics, and culture. It emphasizes that dialogue—not debate—leads to “improvement of experience,” enabling participants to transform knowledge into wisdom and empathy into cooperative action. The introduction of AI demonstrated new possibilities for inclusive, reflective communication on environmental issues, suggesting that human–AI collaboration can enhance environmental literacy and ethical awareness in the pursuit of sustainability.

items.title: How AI Shapes Child Consumer Preferences
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is revolutionizing children's consuming contexts via algorithmic personalization, predictive analytics, and immersive digital platforms. This chapter analyzes the impact of AI-driven marketing methods on child consumer choices, emphasizing persuasive design, data-driven targeting, and behavioral profiling. The discourse emphasizes nascent hazards associated with privacy, data exploitation, and digital well-being, especially considering the cognitive and developmental susceptibilities of children. The chapter examines governance difficulties and advocates for human-centered policy innovation, monitoring and assessment frameworks, and multi-stakeholder engagement to alleviate possible impacts. Future research directions highlight the importance of new technologies and inclusive governance frameworks to foster ethical and responsible digital ecosystems. This chapter elucidates the impact of AI on child consumer behavior, while advocating for human-centered government and child safety.

items.title: How AI threat perception relates to post-adoptive AI agent engagement: the dual paths of self-efficacy and defensive motivation
items.abstract: Introduction As AI evolves into agent-based forms, AI threat perception has become a defining workplace concern. Informed by Cognitive Appraisal Theory and Protection Motivation Theory, this cross-sectional study investigates how AI threat perception relates to post-adoptive AI agent engagement via dual paths of AI self-efficacy and defensive motivation. Methods Semi-structured interviews ( N = 13) first grounded scale adaptation. Structural equation modeling was then conducted on data collected from 387 knowledge workers, followed by multi-group analysis. Results The structural model demonstrates that AI threat perception is indirectly associated with post-adoptive engagement through both mediators, exhibiting an indirect-only pattern. Multi-group analysis further reveals demographic and contextual boundary conditions, showing that higher education significantly amplifies defensive motivation (the link is stronger among postgraduates), while exploratory career-stage and regional comparisons indicate that the self-efficacy pathway is stronger among early-to-mid career professionals and workers in eastern regions. Discussion The study highlights the concurrent coexistence of capability beliefs and defensive intentions in post-adoptive use, while pointing to the need for longitudinal research to trace their temporal dynamics. These findings refine our understanding of technology threat perception and inform human-agent collaboration.

items.title: How Perceived University Support Shapes Marketing Students’ AI Self-Efficacy: A Multigroup Dual-Mediation TAM Analysis Across Three Chinese Universities
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) in marketing has prompted higher education institutions to invest substantially. However, a critical pedagogical question remains: whether and how these institutional investments translate into students’ psychological readiness to deploy AI tools effectively. Students’ AI self-efficacy constitutes a foundational prerequisite for technology adoption and career adaptability. A lack of such confidence can precipitate technology avoidance behaviors and diminish learning engagement. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a cognitive-mediation framework, this study investigates how perceived university support (PUS) shapes marketing students'’ AI self-efficacy (AISE) through the dual mediating beliefs of perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU),and whether this mechanism holds across institutionally heterogeneous settings. Using structural equation modeling with a sample of 538 marketing students from three Chinese universities, we find that PUS significantly enhanced both PU and PEOU in all samples,and that both beliefs carried the effect of support to self-efficacy.PU and PEOU mediated the PUS–AISE relationship: the indirect effect via PEOU was consistently stronger than that via PU,and the direct PUS–AISE path remained significant in two of the three institutions.This study bridges the gap between resource allocation and student psychological outcomes. The robust dual-mediation pathway offers actionable insights for universities: to build student confidence in AI, investments must be channeled not merely into infrastructure but also into pedagogical strategies that demonstrably reduce the perceived complexity of AI tools and illustrate the professional relevance of these tools.Limitations concerning the cross-sectional self-report design and the single-country sample are discussed.

items.title: How Reliable Is LLM Confidence in Hindi and Marathi? A Study of Calibration and Answer Stability
items.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to answer exam-style questions in Indian languages, and their confidence scores are often treated as a signal for when an answer can be trusted. We checked how far that trust is justified for two small open-weight models, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, using 300 native-language multiple-choice questions each in Hindi and Marathi from the MILU benchmark. Confidence was read directly from the probability the model assigns to each answer letter. The 3B model scored 45.0% in Hindi and 32.7% in Marathi while reporting an average confidence above 91%, which gives expected calibration errors (ECE) of 0.483 and 0.592. The Marathi–Hindi difference in ECE had a 95% bootstrap interval of 0.034 to 0.185. Reordering the answer options, a change that leaves the question unchanged, altered the chosen answer for about 38–40% of questions with the 3B model and 52–57% with the 1.5B model, even though overall accuracy and calibration hardly moved. A single temperature parameter fitted on half of the questions brought held-out ECE of the 3B model below 0.1 in both languages, including on reordered options, but it did not improve the model’s ability to separate right answers from wrong ones (AUROC about 0.6). This is a small-scale study of one model family and one prompt format, and we state its limits openly. The main message is practical: an overall accuracy number can look steady while individual answers and confidence scores are not. Keywords: calibration; large language models; Hindi; Marathi; prompt sensitivity; selective prediction; temperature scaling
